A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CTEG and EmoAva study. All 19 pages of each version, including equations, tables, figures and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V3 reports original benchmark experiments, human preference results, ablations and model analyses in Section 6 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V4 retains those original empirical results and additionally reports preference agreement and qualitative failure cases.

M1.justification: The EwA module, variational autoregressive decoder, latent temporal attention, losses and generation procedure remain unchanged. Appendix F proposes anomaly detection and interpolation only as future work.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate on EmoAva and the LM-Listener dataset with the same task coverage. The added failure examples concern existing test outputs and do not establish a distinct test scenario.

E2.justification: LM-Listener, Shuffle and Random retain their respective comparison roles. Comparator membership in the quantitative tables and human preference figure is unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported splits, metrics, training settings and evaluation procedures remain unchanged. Both preference studies use 50 sampled sentences, a maximum sequence length of 128, rendering at 24 frames per second and five participants.

E4.justification: V4 adds Appendix F and Figure 11 examining occasional exaggerated jaw movements in generated expressions. This is a limited qualitative error analysis; the existing ablations and Appendix C analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 5.2 newly reports Fleiss’ kappa of 0.77 for preference agreement. The dataset annotation kappa of 0.86 and bootstrap standard errors using 1,000 iterations were already reported in v3. No increase in runs or participants is stated.

E6.justification: All six tables retain identical numerical contents, and the existing plotted results are unchanged. V4 adds the preference agreement value of 0.77 and qualitative findings of exaggerated jaw movements occurring in isolated frames.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions, distributional assumptions, derivations and metric formulas remain unchanged. The new statement about theoretically unlimited expression diversity is conceptual discussion, without a new formal result or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: CTEG, the 15,000-pair EmoAva dataset, and improved expression diversity, smoothness and emotional consistency.

C2.justification: V4 adds discussion of emotional uncertainty and the continuous representation’s potential expression diversity. Appendix F acknowledges unnatural jaw movements, speculates that overlooked training-data anomalies cause them, and proposes future remedies. The existing language and personalization limitations remain.

D1.justification: The resource hyperlink in footnote 1 changes from the GitHub repository to the project website. V4 also describes the existing FLAME representation as PCA-reduced. Training and hardware disclosures remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish a change in actual resource availability.

R1.justification: The cited works and positioning relative to prior methods remain unchanged. Reference edits add publication page ranges and revise author metadata without introducing different works.

P1.justification: V4 adds short Further Discussions and Acknowledgements sections and Appendix F, shortens the author email block, and makes limited wording corrections such as encoder/decoder terminology. The main narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V4 adds the failure-case Figure 11. V3 Figures 11 and 12 are retained as Figures 12 and 13 with corresponding reference updates. Other changes are limited text reflow and layout adjustments; existing tables and visualizations retain their structure.

improvement.justification: V4 modestly improves transparency by reporting preference agreement in Section 5.2 and showing concrete failures in Appendix F, beyond v3’s successful examples and general limitations. These additions help readers assess reliability and failure behavior. The benefit is limited because failure frequency is unquantified and its proposed cause remains speculative.
